![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223065/assets/f531f2467284ef84e0af0758a8e8554f1e5f72ea08d30d0b80c83076fbe5d7a3.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,0)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(0+t(1-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+t)+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t \\  & =1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+t+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[t+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-(0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-2)$ to the point $(2,4),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,4).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-2+t(4-(-2)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)\cdot (6t-2) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-12t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18{t}^{2}-12t+2)\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-6t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(\sqrt{x-1}+y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(1,2)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(1,2)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(1+t(2-1)),\,(2+t(1-2))⟩ \\  & =⟨1+t,\,2-t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x-1}+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{(1+t)-1}+2-t \\  & =\sqrt{t}-t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt{t}-t+2)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{1/2}-t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}+2)-(0) \\  & =\frac{13}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(4,0)$ to the point $(-4,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =12{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12 \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
